That's one of the heaviest questions a person can ask, and I don't want to wave it away with something glib. Let me look for what grounded sources say about this before responding.I hear the weight behind this question, and I want to be honest with you rather than hand you something tidy that dodges the pain of it. So let me lay out what I found, and where the real tension stays unresolved.

**No answer fully dissolves the horror.** One source, EveryStudent, addresses this almost exactly in your terms — someone asking "why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?" Their response doesn't try to explain away the evil itself: "There is no explanation for such actions... When coming to terms with it, rage is appropriate." That's worth sitting with — even sources trying to give an answer admit some things don't get a satisfying explanation. (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)

**The main line of reasoning offered is human freedom.** That same source argues God gives people freedom to choose, and doesn't override that freedom even when people use it to hurt others — including children: "Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices." It also raises a hard question back: if God stopped every evil act by force, where would that line be drawn, and what would that cost in terms of freedom itself? (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)

**But that doesn't cover everything.** Cru's article distinguishes between suffering caused by human choices (sin) and suffering that isn't anyone's direct fault — a child born with an illness, a natural disaster. Sightline Ministry points to the story of the man born blind, where Jesus explicitly says it wasn't "because of his sins or his parents' sins" — some suffering just is, a byproduct of living in a world with physical laws and brokenness, not a targeted punishment or lesson. (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html; Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)

**What Christianity claims God does about it, rather than just explaining it:** thelife.com makes the point that God didn't stay distant from suffering — in Jesus, "he has given us... a down payment that he does have good reasons for allowing evil." The claim is that God entered into suffering himself through Jesus, rather than simply permitting it from a safe distance: "Though he was innocent, he voluntarily took upon himself the punishment that we deserve." (thelife, https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)

I won't pretend that settles the ache of watching a child suffer — I don't think these sources claim it does either. What they're offering isn't "here's why it's actually fine," but something more like: the evil is real and not God's design, freedom is costly, and God's response was to enter the suffering rather than stay untouched by it.

Where does this question come from for you — is it more of a philosophical wrestling, or is there something painful and specific behind it?

I'm really sorry about your dad. Losing a parent is heavy enough without also carrying this kind of uncertainty about where he is now — that's a deeply painful place to sit, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps returning to it. Let me look into what's actually taught on this so I can give you a grounded answer rather than just guessing.I want to be honest with you about something first: none of the passages I found give a definitive, direct answer to "here's exactly what happens to someone who never went to church." What they do point to, again and again, is that in Christian understanding, it's not church attendance itself that determines what happens after death — it's a person's relationship with Jesus. Let me share what these sources actually say, and I'll be clear about where the gaps are.

One story (Cru, "Forgiving My Dad Set Us Both Free," https://www.cru.org/us/en/blog/life-and-relationships/holidays/forgiving-my-dad-set-us-both-free.html) describes a father who had never had a relationship with Jesus, but shortly before he died, prayed to receive Christ — and the author describes real assurance about where he went afterward. This reflects a common thread in these sources: it's the internal turning toward Jesus, not outward religious practice like church attendance, that these writers see as decisive.

Another piece (thelife, "Finally In His Presence," https://thelife.com/devotionals/finally-in-his-presence) points to Jesus' words to the thief on the cross — a man who, as far as we know, had no religious life at all — telling him "today you will be with me in paradise." The author uses this to say that it's not about a person's track record of religious practice, but about that moment of turning toward Christ, even at the very end.

A third source (thelife, "What Kind of Eternal Life Does Jesus Offer Us?", https://thelife.com/what-kind-of-eternal-life-does-jesus-offer-us) frames it as a relationship — "the Spirit of Christ was in her, and she belonged to him" — again pointing to relationship as the key thing, not church membership.

Here's what I genuinely don't know, and I won't pretend to: I don't have a grounded answer in these sources about what happens to someone whose heart and final moments we simply don't know — where there was no conversation like the one in that first story, no clear moment we witnessed. That's a real gap, and honestly, it's one of the hardest and most tender parts of grief. Many people who love God still wrestle with not knowing, and I don't want to hand you a tidy answer that isn't actually there.

What I can say is this: you loved your dad, and the not-knowing you're carrying is a sign of that love, not a failure on your part. Would it help to talk more about him, or about what's underneath this question for you — is it more about fear, or hope, or something else?

That's a fair question — and the language itself does sound like a contradiction on the surface, so let's unpack what's actually being claimed.

**The key distinction: "essence" vs. "person"**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity," the doctrine states that God is **one in essence** and **three in person**. That's the crucial move: Christians aren't saying God is one *and* three in the *same* sense. As the Spanish-language Cru resource ("Entender la Trinidad") puts it, "solo habría una contradicción si decimos que Dios es tres en la misma forma que él es uno" — there would only be a contradiction if we said God is three in the *same way* he is one. Since he's one in one respect (essence) and three in another respect (person), it's not logically contradictory — more like saying something is one *team* made of three *players*. Not a perfect analogy, but it shows the categories differ.

Cru breaks it into three claims held together:
1. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are **distinct persons** — the Bible shows them relating to one another (e.g., the Father sends the Son into the world in John 3:16; the Father and Son together send the Spirit in John 14:26 and Acts 2:33), so they can't just be the same person wearing different masks.
2. **Each person is fully God** — the Father is called God (Philippians 1:2), Jesus is called God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit is called God (Acts 5:3-4).
3. Yet there is **only one God** — not three gods, because all three share the very same divine essence.

(Source: Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief," https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)

**Some analogies people use (with caveats)**

EveryStudent's article offers a math-style way of picturing it: rather than 1+1+1=3, think of it more like 1×1×1=1 — hence "Tri-unity." They also mention illustrations like water existing as ice, liquid, and steam (all still H2O), or the sun giving off light, heat, and radiation while remaining one sun. The German EveryStudent article ("Dreieinigkeit") uses similar comparisons. But both sources are careful to say **no illustration is perfect** — these are just aids for the imagination, not full explanations.

(Source: EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity? This Article Explains It Simply," https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)

**Why Christians hold onto it despite the mystery**

Cru's article "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?" describes the Trinity as "perhaps the most mysterious, beautiful and confounding doctrine of the Christian faith" and admits that "all human explanations fall short" because "humans are limited in their understanding." The reasoning isn't that Christians invented a paradox for fun — it's that they believe the Bible itself presents God this way: fully one, yet relational within himself, with Father, Son, and Spirit loving and interacting with one another eternally.

(Source: Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?," https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html)

**Bottom line:** It's not "1 = 3" in the same sense (which would be a real contradiction), but "one *what* he is (essence), three *who* he is (persons)." It remains genuinely mysterious — Christians generally don't claim to fully grasp it, just to trust what they believe has been revealed. If you want, I'm happy to dig into any one piece of this further — like the specific Bible passages, or why this doctrine matters practically.

This is a really important question, and it's good you're exploring it thoughtfully.

**Where Christians and Muslims agree and differ**

Both faiths honor Jesus and share some common figures (Abraham, Moses, David), but what each says about who Jesus *is* differs sharply. As one source from Cru puts it: "Muslims believe Jesus to be a prophet but not God in the flesh, whereas Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but the Son of God" (Cru, [What Makes Christianity Different?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html)).

**How Christians understand "Son of God"**

A key clarification Christians often make: this isn't about God having a son in a biological or physical sense — which Islam rightly rejects as incompatible with the oneness of God (tawhid). Instead, as EveryStudent.sk explains, "Christianity understands Jesus' sonship not in a physical sense, but in a spiritual sense. Jesus is God incarnate, who was not born of a physical relationship between a man and woman, but through the miraculous work of the Holy Spirit." The prophet Isaiah foretold this centuries before Jesus' birth, calling the coming child "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (EveryStudent.sk, [Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely](https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)).

**Why Christians see Jesus as more than a prophet**

Christians point to Jesus' own words about himself — "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" — as evidence that he claimed a unique identity, not just a prophetic role (EveryStudent.sk, same article above).

Also central to this difference: "Muslims do not believe in the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, but these are fundamental truths for the Christian faith" (Cru, [What Makes Christianity Different?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html)). Islamic tradition, per the Quran, holds that Jesus was not crucified but was raised to heaven, with someone else crucified in his place (EveryStudent.sk, [Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely](https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)).

**A resource made for this exact conversation**

EveryStudent.com has a dedicated, respectful article for this — explicitly written "with no challenges" and "no criticism of any religion" — addressing questions like "Why not view Jesus as a prophet?" and whether calling God's Son is blasphemy (EveryStudent, [Jesus in Islam](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).

If you're wrestling with this personally — whether from a Muslim background or just curious — I'd love to hear more about what's drawing you to ask. Is there a particular angle (the crucifixion, the nature of "Son of God," something else) you'd like to dig into further?

That's a fair and honest question — and the answer, based on the sources I found, is a bit nuanced: Jesus is never quoted in the Gospels saying the literal sentence "I am God." But there are a few places where his own words, quoted directly, make a very strong claim about his identity. Here's what's actually recorded as coming from his mouth:

**1. John 8:58** — "Very truly I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!"
This is one of the most striking. "I AM" is the name God used for himself when speaking to Moses from the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). According to Jesus Film Project's *40 Interesting Facts about Jesus* (jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts), Jesus is deliberately invoking that divine name for himself here.

**2. John 10:30** — "I and the Father are one."
Per Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god), a Greek scholar's reading of "one" here points to oneness in essence/nature, not just purpose. The immediate reaction from the Jewish leaders listening was to pick up stones to kill him for blasphemy — they clearly heard it as a claim to deity (John 10:31-33, cited via Sightline Ministry, sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god).

**3. Mark 14:61-62** — At his trial, the high priest asks him directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answers, "I am." This is quoted by both Cru (cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html) and Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false). The high priest's reaction was to tear his robes and cry "Blasphemy!" — again, the listeners took it as a direct claim to divine identity.

**4. John 5:17-18** — "My Father is always at his work... and I, too, am working." Sightline Ministry notes that by saying "my Father" rather than "our Father," Jesus put his own activity on equal footing with God's — which is exactly how the religious leaders around him took it, since the text says they then wanted to kill him "because he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God" (John 5:18).

So: no single verse has Jesus saying "I am God" in those exact four words. But in his own quoted speech, he uses the divine name (John 8:58), claims oneness with the Father (John 10:30), and affirms he is the Son of God under direct questioning (Mark 14:61-62) — and the people who heard him firsthand consistently understood these as claims to be God, strongly enough that they wanted to execute him for it.

I'd encourage you to read John 5, 8, and 10, and Mark 14 for yourself in context — that's really the best way to weigh what he meant. Would you like me to dig into any one of these passages more closely?

Your uncle's concern is a really common one, and it's worth taking seriously rather than brushing off — but the evidence actually points the other way.

**Why "too many translations = lost original" isn't quite accurate:**

According to Sightline Ministry, we don't have the *original* manuscripts of the Bible (called "autographs"), but we do have thousands of *copies* (manuscripts). These copies have some differences due to human copying error, but "there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries).

**On translations specifically:**
EveryVietStudent addresses this directly — the concern that the New Testament was translated "too many times" and got corrupted along the way. But actual translations "were made directly from the original Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic based on thousands of ancient manuscripts" — not translations-of-translations-of-translations (https://www.everyvietstudent.com/a/215KinhThanh.html).

**The manuscript evidence itself:**
- We have over 24,000 handwritten manuscript copies of portions of the New Testament (EveryVietStudent, same source above).
- When these manuscripts are compared to each other, they agree word-for-word about 99.5% of the time. Most differences are things like spelling or word order, which barely affect meaning (same source; also EveryStudent, "Jesus in Islam," https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).
- Complete Bibles exist dating back to around 300 A.D., and comparing them to modern Bibles shows they're essentially the same. The Dead Sea Scrolls (ancient Old Testament manuscripts) also confirmed the text has remained "highly similar, nearly 100% identical" over time (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).

**On the "human error" question:**
Sightline Ministry notes that yes, scribes made some copying mistakes over the centuries, but "these changes do not compromise the reliability or accuracy of the Bible we use today. In many cases the changes were obvious, and scholars can identify the original reading with a high degree of confidence" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error).

So the short answer: your uncle's instinct — that ancient texts passed down by hand over centuries could get corrupted — is a fair thing to wonder about. But when you actually look at the manuscript evidence, scholars have far more material to work with for the Bible than for almost any other ancient text, and it shows remarkable consistency. That doesn't "prove" every theological claim in the Bible, but it does mean the text we have today is a well-attested, carefully reconstructed representation of what was originally written.

Would it help to look at a specific example — like a passage your uncle thinks may have been altered — so we can dig into the actual evidence together?

That's one of the most common questions people have about Christianity, and it's a fair one to ask — let me find some grounded material on it.It's a really good question to raise, because on the surface "three" and "one" sound like they can't both be true. Here's how Christians resolve that, based on the sources I found:

**The key distinction: "one" and "three" apply to different things**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief" (https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html), the doctrine means "there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." Stated more precisely: "God is one in essence and three in person." That article lays out three claims held together:
1. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons (not just three names or roles for the same individual).
2. Each Person is fully God.
3. There is still only one God.

The reason this isn't a logical contradiction is that "one" and "three" are being said in *different senses* — one in essence (what God *is*), three in person (*who* God is). A contradiction would only occur if someone claimed God was three in the very same sense he is one. As a related Cru piece on the Trinity puts it (in Spanish, "Entender la Trinidad," https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html): God is one *essence* — essence meaning the same as "being" — so since God is only one essence, he is only one being, not three. The three persons share that one essence rather than each having a separate one.

**Why they say the Persons are distinct, not just "modes"**

The Cru "Understanding the Trinity" article notes the Bible calls the Father God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit God (Acts 5:3-4) — but also treats them as distinct from one another: the Father sends the Son (John 3:16), the Son returns to the Father and then the Father and Son send the Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Since one can send another, they can't simply be the same person wearing different masks.

**Some analogies people use (with the caveat that all fall short)**

EveryStudent's article "What is the Holy Trinity?" (https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html) suggests thinking of it not as 1+1+1=3, but more like 1×1×1=1 — hence the word "Trinity" (tri + unity). It also mentions common illustrations like water existing as ice, liquid, and steam, or the sun's light, heat, and radiation — three expressions, one source — while acknowledging "no illustration is going to be perfect."

Cru's article "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?" (https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html) adds an important honesty: "all human explanations fall short. Humans are limited in their understanding." It frames the Trinity less as a math puzzle to solve and more as a description of a God who is inherently relational — Father, Son, and Spirit "have loved, interacted with and rejoiced over each other for all of eternity."

So the short version: it's not a contradiction because "one" refers to God's essence/being, and "three" refers to persons within that one being — different categories, not the same claim twice. It remains genuinely mysterious, and Christians generally admit that outright rather than pretending it's fully explainable.

Does that distinction between "essence" and "person" make sense, or would it help to dig into one part more — like why Christians believe Jesus himself is called God?

This is a really important question, and one that many Muslims and Christians talk about respectfully with one another. Here's what Christians generally say:

**The core difference:** As Cru explains, "Muslims believe Jesus to be a prophet but not God in the flesh, whereas Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but the Son of God" ([Cru, "What Makes Christianity Different?"](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html)). This same source notes that "Muslims do not believe in the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, but these are fundamental truths for the Christian faith."

**On why Christians see Jesus as more than a prophet, not less:** Christians would say they're not diminishing Jesus's role as a messenger from God, but adding to it. EveryStudent's article "Jesus in Islam" frames it this way — the question isn't "why not view Jesus as a prophet?" but why Christians believe he's *also* the fulfillment of what the prophets pointed toward ([EveryStudent, "Jesus in Islam"](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html)).

**On what "Son of God" actually means:** This is often the biggest sticking point, since Islam firmly rejects the idea that God could have a son as a violation of God's oneness. A Slovak-language resource addresses this directly: Christianity understands Jesus's sonship "not in a physical sense, but in a spiritual sense. Jesus is God incarnate, who was not born of a physical union of a man and woman, but through the miraculous work of the Holy Spirit" ([EveryStudent.sk, "Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely"](https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)). In other words, Christians aren't claiming God had a son the way humans do — they mean Jesus is God's own self, sent among us.

**On the crucifixion:** The same source explains that in Islam, Jesus did not die on the cross — some traditions hold that another was crucified in his place while Jesus was taken up to heaven ([EveryStudent.sk](https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)). For Christians, though, Jesus's death and resurrection are central — not incidental — to who he is and what he accomplished.

If you're wrestling with this yourself — whether from a Muslim background or just curious — I'd love to hear more about what's drawing you to the question. Is it more about the historical claims (did the crucifixion happen?), or more about the theological idea (can God have a son)?

That's a really important question — and a fair one to ask. You're right that the Gospels never quote Jesus saying the literal sentence "I am God." But several passages record him saying things about himself that, in their context, function as exactly that kind of claim. Here are his own recorded words:

**1. "Before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58)**
According to Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god and sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false), Jesus here uses "I am" — the very name God gave himself to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). The reaction was immediate: the crowd picked up stones to kill him for blasphemy, showing they understood exactly what he meant.

**2. "The Father and I are one." (John 10:30)**
Cited by Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god) — the surrounding crowd's response makes the meaning clear: "You, a mere man, claim to be God" (John 10:33, as quoted by Cru at cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html).

**3. At his trial: "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answered, "I am." (Mark 14:61-62)**
Quoted by both Cru (cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html) and Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false). The high priest immediately tore his robes and cried "Blasphemy!" — again, the hearers took it as a direct claim to deity.

**4. "My Father is always working, and so am I." (John 5:16-18)**
Sightline Ministry (sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god) points out that by saying "my Father" rather than "our Father," Jesus placed his own activity on equal footing with God's — and John notes the Jewish leaders wanted to kill him partly because "he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God" (John 5:18).

**5. After the resurrection, Thomas responds to Jesus by saying, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:27-28)**
Jesus does not correct or rebuke him — quoted in Jesus Film Project's article (jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts).

So to directly answer you: no single verse has Jesus saying the plain sentence "I am God." But in John 8:58, John 10:30, and Mark 14:61-62, his own recorded words carry that claim clearly enough that the people who heard him say so understood him to mean exactly that — and responded as though he'd said it outright.

Does it help to look at any one of these passages more closely, or talk about why he might have spoken this way rather than just saying it plainly?

I completely understand that frustration — it's smart to want to trace claims back to real, named sources instead of just trusting a confident-sounding answer. Here are actual pages laying out what Christians believe Jesus' death accomplished, with a quick summary of each so you know what you're clicking into:

1. **"Why did Jesus Have to die?"** — Jesus Film Project
 https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/why-jesus-had-to-die
 Lays out several reasons, starting with the idea that Jesus' death canceled humanity's "debt" of sin — citing Colossians 2:13-14, which says God "canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness... nailing it to the cross."

2. **"What Is Justification and How Does It Work?"** — Cru
 https://www.cru.org/us/en/blog/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/justification.html
 Explains the concept of justification — that Jesus didn't just cancel the debt of sin but actually paid it, quoting Romans 3:23-24 and Galatians 2:16 on being "justified by faith."

3. **"Step 1: The Christian Adventure"** — Cru
 https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/10-basic-steps/1-the-christian-adventure.html
 Describes Jesus' death as bridging "the gulf between the holiness of God and the sinfulness of man," drawing on Colossians 1:13-14 and 1:20-23, and notes that without the resurrection, "His sacrifice would have been incomplete."

4. **"Why Is the Resurrection of Jesus So Important?"** — Jesus Film Project
 https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/resurrection-important
 Connects the resurrection directly to the sufficiency of Jesus' death, arguing (via 1 Corinthians 15 and Hebrews 2:9) that the resurrection was God's "public announcement" that He was satisfied with the sacrifice.

5. **"Why Was Jesus Crucified?"** — Cru
 https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/why-was-jesus-crucified.html
 Focuses on the idea that Jesus' death also defeated death itself and "destroyed the devil's work," citing John 12:30-32 and 1 John 3:8.

Together these sources describe the main themes Christians point to: Jesus' death as payment for sin's debt, as reconciliation with God, as victory over death, and as defeat of evil — with the resurrection completing that work. This is such a common and fair question — and it's worth digging into rather than just taking anyone's word for it (mine included!).

Here's what the sources say:

**The short answer: your uncle raises a real concern, but the evidence actually points the other way.**

It's true we don't have the *original* documents (the actual papyrus or parchment the biblical authors first wrote on) — those wore out or were lost long ago, as **Sightline Ministry** explains: "we don't have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries).

But that's actually true of *all* ancient literature — we don't have Plato's or Aristotle's original manuscripts either. What makes the Bible's case unusually strong is the sheer *quantity* and *closeness in time* of the copies. As **EveryStudent** notes, "there exist today nearly 25,000 hand-written copies of portions of the New Testament," and when historians compare them, "the New Testament we have today is at least 99.5% accurate to the original... The .5% differences refer to spelling, but no change in meaning" (https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html). That same source points out you can compare today's Bible to complete Bibles dating back to 300 A.D. — housed in places like the Vatican and the London Museum — "and the Bible we have today is the same as then."

**Sightline Ministry** adds an important nuance: yes, scribes made copying errors over the centuries — that's just human nature. But "there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error). Because we have so many manuscripts, scholars can spot the mistakes by comparing them against each other — it's like having thousands of witnesses to cross-check rather than relying on just one or two.

The **cadaestudiante.com (EveryStudent Spanish)** source frames the key test well: when judging any ancient document's reliability, we ask "how many copies do we have?" and "how much time passed between the original and the earliest copy we have?" (https://www.cadaestudiante.com/articulos/biblia.html). By those standards, the Bible is actually far better attested than almost any other ancient text we trust historically.

So the "telephone game" image — where a message gets more garbled with each retelling — isn't quite the right picture. It's more like having thousands of independent copies you can lay side by side and compare, which lets scholars trace back with real confidence to what was originally written.

Would you like to dig into how translations specifically work (going from the original Greek/Hebrew into English, for example)? That's a related but slightly different question your uncle might also be pointing at.
